newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean prices ease on good weather.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean prices ease on good weather.

text.p: Nearby prices for Brazilian soybeans dropped as the weather returned to normal in key growing regions and traders predicted a quiet week ahead with many people away for the carnival holiday.

The closure of a bulk export terminal at the port of Paranagua for routine maintenance was also dampening business, although the port was functioning as normal and ships could still load at private terminals.
"In general prices tend to drop off at this time of year," said one trader. "It's a kind of seasonal ebb."

Regular rains returned to the key growing region of Rio Grande do Sul this week after a mostly dry December and January, restoring soil moisture levels and alleviating fears of a drop in the state's crop.
Meanwhile, rains eased in Mato Grosso, allowing farmers to proceed with the harvest of the so-called precocious cycle crop.
"We've been able to harvest practically every day this week," said Tony Fagundes at the Cooperlucas cooperative. "About 15 percent of the total (early cycle) crop has been harvested."
In Parana, heavy rains which had threatened to cause crop damage also fizzled out and conditions were near-ideal with warm weather and high humidity.
Fears that a delay in early shipments could clog up Paranagua had now abated and trade should be brisk in the week following carnival, one trader said.
Independent consultant Safras e Mercado said that 31 percent of the 1996/97 crop had already been committed in the week ending on Jan 30, up from 21 percent in the same period last year.
"Considering a crop of 26.3 million tonnes, we would have a traded volume close to 8.2 million tonnes," it said. "From this total, about 56 percent is from the states of Parana and Mato Grosso."

"Business is being done," said a trader, adding that he had heard around 200,000 tonnes of soybeans were traded for March, April and May shipment on Thursday, although he did not have any details on the destination.
Crushers continued to offer soybeans for quick cash as the abolition of the ICMS export tax made it more profitable to export soybeans that soymeal or soyoil, traders said.
"It's not a very good thing for Brazil anyway because someone else will make a profit on processing the beans abroad," the trader said.

The Brazilian Vegetable Oils Industries Association (ABIOVE) earlier reported that member firms crushed 917,000 tonnes of soybeans in December, down from 1.3 million in November. This represented 84 to 86 percent of total Brazilian crushings, it estimated.
The December figure left industry stocks at 751,000 tonnes, down from 1.34 million at the end of November, ABIOVE said.
